extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of narratology; advanced creative writers and literary critics studying narrative technique
extracted.subtask_description: Identify, analyze, and apply narratological categories (mood/voice, focalization, reported speech, interior/free indirect style, objectivized character language) to fictional texts. Emphasizes distinctions between who sees (focalization) and who speaks (narratorial voice) and practical effects in example passages (Proust, Balzac, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reported inner speech and gradations of indirect style
rubrics_metrics.description: The text identifies a spectrum of modalities between narrated speech, subordinated indirect style, and free indirect style whereby a narrator reports a character's thoughts with varying degrees of mediation (e.g., narrator describing Swann's feelings, then subordinated indirect style, then lending his voice in free indirect style).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attend to surface markers and grammatical transpositions that signal shifts (phrases like 'He had the sudden suspicion' introducing indirect style; later passages where narrator 'lends his voice' constitute free indirect style). Examples: passages from Swann where sequences of thoughts are reported in indirect style and then the narrator adopts Swann's inner speech in free indirect style. These gradations are subtle and can be blended imperceptibly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Free indirect style
rubrics_metrics.description: A mode in which the narrator 'lends' his voice to a character's inner speech, including the grammatical transpositions that this implies, producing a speech that is at once characterial and narrated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for the combination of third-person narration with the character's idiom and intensities (theatrical rhetoric, exclamations, self-address). In Proust, free indirect style is used especially in moments of ardent emotion; it is marked by the narrator's adoption of the character's tone without explicit quotation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reported inner monologue versus authentic interior monologue
rubrics_metrics.description: Proustian 'inner speech' is largely reported and managed by the narrator rather than the modern 'interior monologue' which encloses character subjectivity in an infra‑verbal inchoate flux; Proust largely avoids the 'hodgepodge' of infraverbal stream-of-consciousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate passages where thought is presented as a demonstration or narratorial handling (e.g., madeleine episode) from passages that attempt linguistic minimalism and inchoateness. The presence of narrator control, logical coherence, or philosophical stance suggests reported inner speech rather than authentic interior monologue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insincere monologue uttered aloud (inner speech as performance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters sometimes speak 'to themselves, aloud' in public or in the street; these perorations are theatrical, often insincere, and function as a performed 'comedy' masking different inner motives (e.g., Swann's loud invective that actually masks a desire to reingratiate).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat public self-address as a clue to duplicity: the content, intonation, and performative force may diverge from the 'felt truth' and reveal social strategy rather than authentic thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phonetic and intonational features as part of thought
rubrics_metrics.description: The sound of the voice and its intonation can be part of what thought 'is' in the text; fictitious intonation can reveal insincerity or other dimensions of mental life beyond lexical content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analysing inner speech, include prosodic markers (reported tone, theatricality, stiltedness). In examples the artificial sonority of a character's own voice reveals discrepancy between expressed words and underlying concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objectivized character language (stylistic autonomy / idiolect)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proust grants characters linguistic autonomy—an 'objectivized' language—so that characters may speak with distinctive idiolects or sociolectal marks (Anglicisms, archaisms, puns, group pronunciations), differentiating narrator speech and character speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify recurring linguistic tics, sociolectal markers, borrowings, or stylized pastiche that make a character's speech autonomous. Examples range from minimal connotative markers to full-blown personal styles (Odette's Anglicisms; Charlus's rhetoric).

rubrics_metrics.name: Levels of stylistic individuation in characterization
rubrics_metrics.description: Three levels of linguistic individuation: (1) minimal connotative relationship (occasional slips, dialectal features), (2) recurrent characteristic/tic forming a stable marker of character, (3) full personal style or stylized pastiche where 'imitation' becomes hyperbolic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this hierarchy to assess how language contributes to character: whether it only signals social/class belonging, forms a recurrent tic that aids recognition, or becomes a sustained idiolect that risks caricature and circularity (author imitating character imitating author).

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of hyperbolic mimesis (speech as self-disappearance)
rubrics_metrics.description: When mimetic objectivization of speech is pushed to an extreme, it can become caricatural and self-referential—characters 'talk like themselves' to the point that speech becomes a sign pointing back to the text, risking the character's dissolution into his own language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware overdoing stylistic imitation: excessive pastiche may produce a convincing surface yet accentuate psychological evanescence. Critical reading should note circularity (speech quoting the text that quotes it). The narrator's grandmother's remark that Legrandin 'talks a little too much like a book' is emblematic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between mood (focalization) and voice (narratorial identity)
rubrics_metrics.description: A central analytic distinction: mood/focalization = who sees (the point of view that regulates information); voice = who speaks (the identity and distance of the narrator). The two are often confused in prior typologies and must be treated separately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When classifying narrative situations, ask separately 'who sees?' and 'who speaks?'. Avoid conflating first-/third-person narration with focalization; e.g., a narrator can be a character and yet occupy an external focal position, or a third-person narrator can be internally focalized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narratorial voice types (auktoriale, Ich, personale, omniscient etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Typology of narrator identity including the omniscient/auktorial narrator, first-person narrator (Ich-Erzählsituation), and personale Erzähl situation (third-person narrative conducted according to a character's point of view).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these categories to describe narrator presence and authorial intrusions (Fielding vs Hardy). Remember that these voice categories concern who speaks and the narrator's relation to the story, not necessarily focalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focalization (narrative perspective) — tripartition
rubrics_metrics.description: Three-term typology of focalization: (1) zero or nonfocalized narrative (vision from behind; Narrator > Character; classical omniscient), (2) internal focalization (Narrator = Character; restricted field: the narrator says only what a given character knows), (3) external focalization (Narrator < Character; objective/behaviorist narrative that says less than characters know).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt the term 'focalization' to avoid misleading visual metaphors. Determine whether narrative information is greater than, equal to, or less than a character's knowledge. Examples: zero-focalization = classical omniscient narration; internal focalization = The Ambassadors, What Maisie Knew; external focalization = Hammett, many adventure openings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subtypes of internal focalization: fixed, variable, multiple
rubrics_metrics.description: Internal focalization can be (a) fixed — the narrative consistently follows one character's point of view (canonical example: The Ambassadors), (b) variable — focal character shifts across sections (e.g., Madame Bovary alternating Charles and Emma), (c) multiple — several characters provide distinct focal accounts (epistolary novels, The Ring and the Book, Rashomon-like structures).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify internal focalization in terms of stability and number of focalizers. Note that multiple focalization can produce successive perspectives on the same events, useful for dramatizing subjectivity or unreliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: External focalization and its rhetorical uses
rubrics_metrics.description: Narration that remains outside characters' consciousness (external focalization) is often used to create enigma, mystery, or a circumspect, riddle-like effect; common in detective/adventure narratives and in openings that make a character mysterious (Phileas Fogg examples).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize external focalization by absence of access to thoughts/feelings. Use it to sustain suspense, withhold information deliberately, or present characters as enigmatic objects of observation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between focal character (reflector) and narrator
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not conflate the focal character who 'sees' or 'reflects' events with the narrator who 'tells' them; formulations that blur 'story told as if by a character but told in the third person' risk confusion between reflector and narrator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing 'reflector' situations (Friedman's 'Portrait of the Artist' example), maintain separate accounts of focal position and narratorial voice; identify whether the textual 'lens' belongs to a character or to the narrating presence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reported speech vs mimetic dialogue (objectivization vs transfusion of voices)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proust tends toward Balzacian 'reported speech' and 'objectivized language' where characters' speech is given autonomy and separated from the narrator's voice, rather than the Flaubertian ambiguous transfusion of speech/voice; free indirect mixing in dialogue is rare for Proust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess dialogues for clear demarcation (quotation/character autonomy) versus blended, ambiguous voice. Proust's reluctance to adopt servant lexicon without quotation marks is an example of his caution in mixing voices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of dream and infralinguistic sequences to signal logical rupture
rubrics_metrics.description: Incoherent infralinguistic sequences (dream-speech: e.g., 'dear, deer, Francis Jammes, fork') do not represent a privileged dream language of depth but indicate a rupture or incomprehension between two logics—the dream logic and waking alert consciousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret bizarre or incoherent dream utterances not as direct windows into unconscious content but as markers of transition between distinct logical orders; the narrator often interprets/frames these sequences upon waking to show changed transparency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial intrusions and narrator reliability (voice distance)
rubrics_metrics.description: The presence or absence of authorial intrusions (Fielding vs Hardy) and the dramatization or reliability of the narrator form part of 'voice' analysis; distance and implied author considerations affect how the narrative presents knowledge and judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note authorial commentary, intrusions, and signs of a dramatized or unreliable narrator. These are voice phenomena distinct from focalization but crucial to a full account of narrative situation; compare examples where omniscience is accompanied or not by explicit authorial asides.
